text:
@LawrenceTimme  I didn't get to experience the very early days of X99 as I got mine in 2018 from someone that was moving to Ryzen for the content and didn't buy X99 for the platform but the cores.  At first I bought for the cores but over the years I came to realize the value that X99 really was and that we will sadly probably never see again.
I started with a 6800K and 4x 4GB modules (that cost me an outrageous $164).  Just one year later and memory prices were sane again so I picked up 4x 8GB modules for $90 and plopped them in next to my other 4 for a total of 48GB.  On babies first socket, I would have been limited to four sticks.
I then used up all my available PCIE lanes (the 6800k is limited to just 28 of the 40 total on the platform) so I upgraded to an i7-5960X.  A bit over a year later, I burned out the cache on it and needed a replacement so I got a Xeon E5-1660V3 (the same thing I had but with ECC support).
Then a bit of time rolls by and I find out a friend has a bunch of 2133 32GB ECC RDIMMs so I pick up 8 off him on the cheap (like half what I paid for the 48GB).  So now I have 8 core CPU instead of 6, 256GB of RAM instead of 16GB and 4 NVME drives that I can access simultaneously at full speed while consumer socket boards are struggling to find a way to share resources to have more than 2 or 3.
Then while I am doing my best to wait for a reasonable upgrade path from X99, $205 sale price Ryzen 7 5700X3D gets my attention and I find an X570 Taichi that at least gives me two physical CPU PCIE slots even though it is not as much as I wanted, I decide at that low of a price and that much faster a CPU, I would give it a shot and move my X99 to be home server.
So now I have a 5700x3d, 64GB 3200CL16, RTX 3080 desktop with a dual port 25Gb network card that connects to another of the same card in my X99 system - only now it has a Xeon E5-2697A V4 16 core (sadly locked SKU unlike the 1600x), the 256GB RAM, sixteen 4TB SAS HDDs with the HBA passed thru to a Truenas VM via Proxmox and I have 10x 240GB SSDs on the way that I am going to stripe into a 2TB read cache for the HDDs (two RaidZ3 8 disk VDEVs).

But what I really wanted was for AMD to not have murdered TR4 to put HEDT core count CPUs on consumer socket.  I would have bought a 16 core Zen 2 part on TR4 and then again with Zen 3 x3d.  But since more than 8 cores is pure luxury like more than 4 cores was for the longest time, I'm only looking for 16 cores.  And unfortunately AMD still won't offer that to me on the correct platform and intel is also pulling this insane pricing CPUs on both consumer and larger sockets.  It's a terrible time to be a hardware enthusiast unless you want a half computer.

text:
For reference, the RX 480 8GB was released in 2016 at $229.99, which is equivalent to approximately $311.42 USD today, according to the BLS. The 480 has a 232 mm² die with a 256-bit memory bus on GlobalFoundries 14nm. In comparison, the RX 9060 XT has a 199 mm² die with a 128-bit memory bus on TSMC 4nm. At their respective launches, 14nm was roughly two to three times less expensive (in 2016) per wafer than TSMC 4nm is in 2025. If you can get it at MSRP, which is surprisingly possible, you're paying 12.4% more for 16.6% less silicon.

Hard as it may be to believe, the margins on the 9060 XT 16GB are likely substantially slimmer than the margins on the 480 at launch; they're certainly not any better. GPUs in the $300-$350 price segment are legitimately the new performance tier, and this isn't some freak anomaly caused by excessive enterprise demand, miners, or anything like that. When you account for the rising manufacturing costs and the state of our currencies, we're lucky it's not worse. And to be painfully clear about this, it will get worse .

I'm not sure how or why it happened, but the RX 9060 XT 16GB is legitimately another RX 480 8GB in terms of performance per dollar, even at 10% above MSRP. We're just poorer, and the silicon is drastically more expensive. The RX 9070 at $550 is an even better value at/near MSRP, but I haven't seen it below $700 anywhere. I can tolerate a 10% markup, but 30% truly kills the value proposition. At real-world prices, you're paying 50% price for > 60% of 9070 performance and 100% of the VRAM.

MSRP today AMD or Nvidia sets the 'run end' clearance price floor. There are two industry terms for Fake PR price. The first industry term that is a production economic term is 3rd degree consumer discriminatory pricing of 'run end' that at launch are 'lottery units' pulled forward in the supply schedule and sold at MSRP to set run end price. The practice is discriminatory to consumers on the few who can snag one at launch for MSRP and those who cannot but wanted one and left out.

Those who cannot or will not, then may pay a 1st degree consumer discriminatory price at launch that is highest to lower over time on supply and demand and usually associated professional computer products price for that early performance benefit. The other option is secondary consumer discriminatory price where the card you want is thrown into a bundle for some price deal that may or may not be a good deal. 

The other industry terms for 3rd degree 'run end' price discrimination is SEP which means Sales Exit Price which in MSRP examples actually state the ODM/AIB price floor under which enters price less than card cost sales and AMD and Nvidia don't want to get caught up in that.
